nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: Why is PLA considered a popular choice in the bioplastics industry?
nodes.answer: PLA is widely used as a bioplastic due to being completely biodegradable and serving as an alternative to traditional plastics.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How does the environmental impact of the novel biocomposite compare to its counterparts?
nodes.answer: The novel biocomposite generally has higher environmental impacts than conventional antibacterial materials like virgin PLA, fossil-based polypropylene (PP), and high-density polyethylene (HDPE).
nodes.paragraph: To further enhance antibacterial proper - ties and sustainability performance, a novel biocomposite based on PLA with hemp hurd filled with silver nanoparticles (AgNP) was developed. Here we present a life cycle assessment (LCA) based on ISO 14040 and 14044 to evaluate the added value of the antibacterial biocomposite compared to conventional antibacterial materials from an environmental perspective. The environmental impacts are analyzed in comparison to virgin PLA, fossil-based polypropylene (PP) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE) combined in a disinfecting wipes and sterilized application. Our results show that the novel biocomposite has in general higher environmental impacts than its counterparts. Notably, our findings suggest a significant impact derived from high energy demand required for AgNP synthesis. To be able to compete with other materials, the energy demand needs to be minimized, which should be the focus of further research. nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_002
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is the main motivation behind the analysis of bio-based antibacterial plastics based on PLA?
nodes.answer: The main motivation is to analyze if there is an added environmental value compared to conventional materials, which lack inherent antibacterial properties and require separate treatments.
nodes.paragraph: The use of novel bio-based antibacterial plas - tics based on PLA can mitigate the dependence on fossil resources and simultaneously the antibacterial property minimizing the transmission of diseases. The motivation of this work is to analyze if there is an added environmental value compared to conventional materials, which do not have an inherent antibacterial property, hence necessitat - ing a separate treatment. Embedding silver nanoparticles (AgNP) in biopolymers inhibits microbial growth and enhances water vapor permeability, extending product shelf life. These AgNP improve the barrier capabilities, mechani - cal properties, and UV resistance of biopolymers such as PLA, whereas their antimicrobial activity is dictated by their shape, size, and surface charge. Thermal extrusion is an appropriate method of compounding AgNP with PLA [ 5]. For example, Momeni et al. analyzed the effect of inclusion of 1.5 wt.% AgNP on surface, chemical, thermal, and bio - compatibility aspects of PLA bionanocomposites produced via melt mixing. They demonstrated enhanced stability and antimicrobial properties in resultant bionanocomposites [ 6]. Here we consider an antibacterial polylactide-hemp- nanosilver-biocomposite (AgNP-HH-PLA) to address the aforementioned challenge.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_003
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: How are biopolymers classified according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Biopolymers are classified into three groups based on origin and degradability: (1) bio-based and non-biodegradable, (2) bio-based and biodegradable, and (3) fossil-based and biodegradable.
nodes.paragraph: An overview of this data can be found in SI1. AgNPs are only an additive to gain antibacte - rial activity, while the main structure of the novel material is a biocomposite. Biocomposites are compounds made from biopolymers and a natural fiber reinforcing the biopoly - mer. The biopolymers can be classified into three groups, based on their origin (= feedstock) and their degradability (= end-of-life): (1) Bio-based and non-biodegradable: as long-lasting as possible; e.g. bio-polyethylene (bio-PE), bio-propylene (bio-PP); (2) Bio-based and biodegradable: synthesized from renewable raw materials and degradable; e.g. PLA; within biodegradable materials, compostable materials can be differentiated: some materials, like PLA, are degradable in industrial plants but they cannot rot in the compost. (3) fossil-based and biodegradable: conventional polymers, e.g., polycaprolactone (PCL). For bio-based plastics, renewable resources such as sugar, starch, vegetable oils or cellulose are the source, as well as substances of animal origin (e.g., chitin) [ 21, 22].

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the advantages of enzymatic hydrolysis over other chemical processes for degrading PET?
nodes.answer: Enzymatic hydrolysis yields TPA and EG, the monomers used to generate new PET polymers, and follows a first-order kinetics equation, offering a sustainable approach to fabric recycling.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_005
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: Are all natural fibres biodegradable?
nodes.answer: Yes, most natural fibres like cotton, wool, and silk are biodegradable, meaning they can break down naturally in the environment without causing harm.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why is polyester clothing a concern for plastic pollution?
nodes.answer: Clothing made from polyester fibres is non-biodegradable and can take up to 200 years to biodegrade, leading to plastic pollution. Additionally, microfibres shed from polyester clothing can enter water courses and the food chain, posing harm to the human digestive system.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Plastic waste reduction|Biodegradable plastics_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does polyester contribute to environmental pollution?
nodes.answer: Polyester fibres are non-biodegradable and can take up to 200 years to biodegrade, leading to environmental pollution. This can have long-lasting negative effects on the environment.
